docs.label: Documentation & reports
docs.intro: From a blank page to a clean, professional report. Read the lessons in order — each one builds on the last.

lessons.title: Why good writing matters
lessons.lead: Your report is how examiners see your work. Great code with a messy report loses marks. A clear report makes good work look great.

items.title: Clear
items.text: One idea per sentence. The reader never has to guess what you mean.

items.title: Concise
items.text: Say it in fewer words. Cut anything that does not help the reader.

items.title: Correct
items.text: Right facts, right numbers, right grammar, right references.

blocks.text: Write for a busy reader. Your examiner may read 40 reports. Make yours the easiest one to read — that alone puts you ahead.

lessons.title: The documents you will write
lessons.lead: A software project usually needs several documents. Each one has a different job.

items.title: Project proposal
items.text: Before you start. What problem, why it matters, your plan and timeline.

items.title: Requirements (SRS)
items.text: What the system must do (functional) and how well (non-functional).

items.title: Design document
items.text: Architecture, database (ER diagram), and key screens.

items.title: Final report
items.text: The full story: problem, method, build, testing, results, conclusion.

items.title: README
items.text: How to install, run and use your code. Lives in your Git repository.

items.title: User manual
items.text: Step-by-step help for users, with screenshots.

blocks.text: Always read the **marking scheme** first. It tells you exactly which sections the examiner wants to see — and how many marks each one is worth.

lessons.title: How to start (beat the blank page)
lessons.lead: Nobody writes a report from the first word to the last. Here is the order that works.

items.title: Read the brief and marking scheme
items.text: Note every required section and the word or page limit.

items.title: Collect your material
items.text: Screenshots, diagrams, test results, notes, and links to sources you used.

items.title: Write the outline first
items.text: Put down all the headings and sub-headings. This is your skeleton.

items.title: Fill in the easiest section first
items.text: Usually Methodology or Implementation — you already know what you did.

items.title: Write the Introduction and Conclusion next
items.text: Now you know the full story, so they are easy to write.

items.title: Write the Abstract last
items.text: It is a short summary of everything, so it must come at the end.

items.title: Rest, then edit
items.text: Leave it for a day. Fresh eyes catch far more mistakes.

blocks.text: A bad first draft is normal and fine. You cannot edit a blank page — just get the words down, then make them better.

lessons.title: The structure of a project report
lessons.lead: Most project reports follow the same shape. Each section answers one question for the reader.

blocks.text: The **abstract** is the most-read part of your report. Make it 150–250 words: the problem, what you did, the main result, and what it means.

lessons.title: Which tense to use (and where)
lessons.lead: This is the question students ask most. The rule is simple: use the tense that matches the time of the action.

head: Section
Tense
Example
rows: A pilot **was carried out** with 120 students.
Students **lose** items on campus every week.
Earlier systems **focused** on… / Studies **have shown** that…
Data **was collected** through an online survey.
The average time **fell** from 14 to 3 days.
These results **suggest** that alerts help most.

blocks.text: What is the **past participle**? It is the verb form used after *was/were* and *has/have*: collect → **collected**, write → **written**, test → **tested**, choose → **chosen**. In reports you use it all the time in the passive voice: “The system **was tested**”, “Three methods **were compared**”.
Do not jump between tenses inside one paragraph about the same action. Pick the right tense for that section and stay with it.

questions.why: The methodology describes what you already did, so use past tense (passive: was + past participle).
What the report itself does is always true while someone reads it — use present tense.

questions.q: Results: “The average recovery time ___ from 14 to 3 days.”
questions.why: Results describe what happened in your study, so use past tense.

questions.q: Discussion: “These results ___ that instant alerts help the most.”
questions.why: Your interpretation is your current view, so the discussion uses present tense.

lessons.title: Active and passive voice
lessons.lead: Both are correct. The trick is knowing when to use each one.

items.bad: Active: We tested the API with 50 requests.
items.good: Passive: The API was tested with 50 requests.
items.why: Passive puts the focus on the action, not on you. Common in Methodology and Results.

items.bad: Passive: It was decided by the team that Flutter would be used.
items.why: Active is shorter and clearer. Use it when the passive sounds heavy or confusing.

items: **Use passive** when the action matters more than who did it (methods, tests, results).
**Use active** when it makes the sentence shorter and clearer.
Check your university’s rules — some allow “we”, others do not. Never use “I think” or “I feel”.

lessons.title: Write clean and professional sentences
lessons.lead: Small changes make your writing sound professional. Compare each pair below.

items.bad: The app didn’t crash and it’s really fast.
items.good: The application did not crash, and pages loaded in under one second.
items.why: No contractions (didn’t, it’s). Replace vague words like “really fast” with real numbers.

items.bad: Due to the fact that the database was slow, we made an index.
items.good: Because the database was slow, an index was added.
items.why: “Due to the fact that” = “because”. Shorter is better.

items.bad: I think the system is kind of good for students.
items.good: The results show that the system helps students recover items faster.
items.why: No “I think” or “kind of”. Back every claim with evidence.

items.bad: The system has a lot of cool features and stuff.
items.good: The system has four main features: photo upload, a campus map, safe claiming and an admin dashboard.
items.why: Formal words only. Be specific — name the things.

items.bad: In this project which we did for our final year we built a system that is used by students to report items that they lost and also items they found on the campus.
items.good: This project developed a system that lets students report lost and found items on campus.
items.why: One idea per sentence. Long sentences tire the reader.

items.bad: Users, students, and customers can log in.
items.good: Students can log in. (Use the same word every time.)
items.why: Pick one term and use it consistently. Changing words confuses the reader.

do: Keep sentences under about 25 words
Use numbers and facts
Explain every short form once: “Software Requirements Specification (SRS)”
Use the same term for the same thing
dont: Contractions (don’t, can’t, it’s)
Slang or emotional words (awesome, super, cool)
Exclamation marks!
“I think”, “I feel”, “obviously”

lessons.title: Formatting that looks professional
lessons.lead: Good formatting makes your report easy to scan. Keep it simple and consistent.

head: Item
A safe standard
rows: Times New Roman or Calibri — one font for the body
On every page except the title page
Generate it automatically from your headings

blocks.text: Use your word processor’s **Heading 1 / Heading 2 styles** instead of making text bold by hand. Then the table of contents, numbering and navigation all work automatically.

do: Use the same style for every heading level
Leave white space between sections
Align text consistently (justified or left)
dont: Mix many fonts and colours
Use huge blocks of text with no headings
Put a heading alone at the bottom of a page

lessons.title: Figures, tables and diagrams
lessons.lead: A good diagram can replace a page of text — but only if it is labelled and explained.

items: **Figure** captions go **below** the figure. **Table** captions go **above** the table.
Number them in order: Figure 1, Figure 2… and Table 1, Table 2…
Mention every figure in the text: “Figure 3 shows the system architecture.”
Make screenshots readable — crop them and zoom in on what matters.
For software projects, include: use-case diagram, ER diagram, architecture diagram, and key screenshots.

lessons.title: References and avoiding plagiarism
lessons.lead: Every idea, picture or fact that is not yours needs a reference. This protects you and shows good research.

head: Style
In the text
In the reference list
rows: [1] I. Sommerville, Software Engineering, 10th ed. Pearson, 2016.
Sommerville, I. (2016). Software engineering (10th ed.). Pearson.

items: **Paraphrase**: read the source, close it, then write the idea in your own words — and still cite it.
Use quotation marks for exact words, and keep quotes short.
Use a reference manager (Zotero, Mendeley) or Word’s built-in citations.
Prefer good sources: textbooks, official documentation, academic papers.

blocks.text: Copying text and changing a few words is still plagiarism. Write from your understanding, not from the screen.

lessons.title: Technical writing for software projects
lessons.lead: Technical writing explains how something works so another person can use or rebuild it.

items: **Explain why, not only what**: “PostgreSQL was chosen because the data is relational.”
**Do not paste long code**. Show a short, important snippet (10–20 lines) and explain it. Put full code in an appendix or your repository.
**Describe APIs clearly**: the method, the URL, what you send, what you get back.
**Use diagrams** for architecture, data and flows.

blocks.title: A clear README skeleton
blocks.code:
# FindIt — Campus Lost & Found

## What it does
One place for students to report lost and found items, with automatic matching.

## Tech stack
Flutter · ASP.NET Core · PostgreSQL

## How to run it
1. Clone the repository
2. Copy appsettings.example.json to appsettings.Local.json and add your database password
3. Run the API:   dotnet run
4. Run the app:   flutter run

## Team
Group 07 — A. Perera, B. Silva, C. Fernando, D. Jayasinghe

lessons.title: Final checklist before you submit
lessons.lead: Tick these off one by one. Your progress is saved on this device.

items: Every section in the marking scheme is included
The abstract is 150–250 words and written last
Correct tense in every section (past for what you did)
No contractions, slang or “I think”
All figures and tables are numbered, captioned and mentioned in the text
Every source is cited and listed in one reference style
Headings use styles and the contents page is up to date
Page numbers are on every page
Spell check done — and read aloud once
A friend has read it and nothing confused them

present.label: Presentations
present.intro: How to plan, design and deliver a presentation people remember — and how to stay calm in the viva.

lessons.title: What makes a great presentation
lessons.lead: A great presentation has three parts. Most students only work on the slides — the other two matter just as much.

items.title: The story
items.text: A clear path: problem → solution → proof → what’s next. One key message.

items.title: The slides
items.text: Simple visuals that support you. They are not your script.

items.title: The delivery
items.text: Your voice, eye contact and confidence. This is what people remember.

blocks.text: You are the presentation. The slides are only there to help the audience follow you.

lessons.title: Plan before you make slides
lessons.lead: Open PowerPoint last, not first. Plan the message on paper.

items.title: Know your audience
items.text: Examiners want to see the problem, your solution, proof it works, and that you understand it.

items.title: Write your one key message
items.text: One sentence the audience should remember. Example: “FindIt returns lost items four times faster.”

items.title: Plan your time
items.text: About 1 minute per slide. A 10-minute talk ≈ 8–10 slides.

items.title: Sketch the slides on paper
items.text: One idea per slide. Write the headline of each slide first.

items.title: Then build the slides
items.text: Use one clean template, big text and visuals.

lessons.title: A proven outline for project presentations
lessons.lead: Use this order for a 10-minute final-year presentation. It works for almost any project.

blocks.text: Download the example presentation below — it follows this exact outline, with speaker notes on every slide.

lessons.title: Slide design rules
lessons.lead: Good slides are simple. If the audience is reading, they are not listening to you.

do: One idea per slide
Titles that say the point: “Recovery time fell by 78%”
Big text — at least 24 pt
Strong contrast (dark text on light, or light on dark)
Pictures, diagrams and charts instead of paragraphs
One template and 2–3 colours across all slides
dont: Full sentences and paragraphs
More than about 6 short lines of text
Tiny fonts or busy backgrounds
Many animations and sound effects
Different fonts and colours on every slide
Reading your slides word for word

lessons.title: Bad slide vs good slide
lessons.lead: Same content, two very different results. Look at what changed.

lessons.title: How to deliver it
lessons.lead: How you say it matters as much as what you say.

items.title: Eye contact
items.text: Look at people, not at the screen. Move your eyes around the room.

items.title: Slow down
items.text: Nervous people talk fast. Speak slower than feels natural.

items.title: Pause
items.text: Pause after an important point. Silence makes it stick.

items.title: Clear voice
items.text: Speak to the back of the room. Change your tone — no flat voice.

items.title: Body language
items.text: Stand tall, face the audience, use open hand gestures.

items.title: No script
items.text: Know your points, not every word. Use short notes if you must.

lessons.title: Beat the nerves
lessons.lead: Everyone feels nervous. The goal is not to remove the nerves — it is to perform well anyway.

items: **Practise out loud** at least three times, with a timer. Practice is the best cure.
**Know your first 30 seconds by heart.** A strong start calms you down.
**Breathe slowly** before you begin: in for 4 seconds, out for 6.
**Arrive early** and test the projector, laptop and demo.
Remember: the audience wants you to do well.

lessons.title: The live demo
lessons.lead: The demo is the most exciting part — and the most risky. Prepare for things to go wrong.

items: Practise the exact demo steps until they are smooth.
Prepare test data and accounts **before** you start. Stay logged in.
Record a **backup video** of the demo in case the internet or app fails.
Zoom in so everyone can see. Close other apps and turn off notifications.
Talk while you click: “Now I report a lost wallet… and here is the match.”

blocks.text: Show one full user journey from start to finish. That is far stronger than clicking through every screen.

lessons.title: Handling questions and the viva
lessons.lead: Questions are a chance to show you really understand your work.

items.title: Listen to the whole question
items.text: Do not interrupt. It is fine to ask them to repeat it.

items.title: Pause and think
items.text: A short pause looks confident, not weak.

items.title: Answer briefly and directly
items.text: Answer the question first, then add one supporting detail.

items.title: If you do not know, say so
items.text: “I am not sure, but I would find out by…” Never make up an answer.

head: Common viva question
What a good answer includes
rows: Why did you choose this technology?
A real reason linked to your needs (speed, team skills, features).
One honest challenge and how you solved it.
Types of tests, numbers, and what you found.
One or two realistic next steps.
Explain this part of your code.
Walk through it simply. Know every part you wrote.

lessons.title: Bad habits to avoid
lessons.lead: These mistakes are very common. Check that you are not doing any of them.

do: Start with a hook (a question, a number, a short story)
Finish on time — practise with a timer
End by repeating your key message
dont: Starting with “Hello, my name is… and today…” and nothing else
Turning your back to read the screen
Saying “um” and “so yeah” again and again
Apologising: “Sorry, this slide is messy”
Going over time
Ending with “That’s it, I guess.”

lessons.title: Rehearsal checklist
lessons.lead: Tick these off before presentation day. Your progress is saved on this device.

items: My one key message is clear
Each slide has one idea and a headline title
Text is at least 24 pt and easy to read
I practised out loud 3+ times with a timer
I finish inside the time limit
My demo works and I have a backup video
I can answer the 5 common viva questions
Every team member knows their part and can explain the whole system
I checked the room, projector and laptop early

git.label: Git & GitHub
git.intro: Save every version of your code, work as a team without overwriting each other, and show examiners a professional project history. No experience needed — start at lesson 1.

lessons.title: What are Git and GitHub?
lessons.lead: Git is like “save game” for your code. GitHub is the online place where your saves live, so your team can share them.

items.title: Git
items.text: A program on YOUR computer. It records every change to your files, so you can go back in time.

items.title: GitHub
items.text: A website that stores your Git project online. Your team pulls and pushes changes there.

items.title: Commit
items.text: One saved snapshot of your project, with a message saying what changed.

items.title: Repository (repo)
items.text: One project folder tracked by Git — all files plus all their history.

blocks.text: Examiners and employers **look at your commit history**. Small, regular commits from every team member show real teamwork. One giant commit the night before the deadline shows the opposite.

lessons.title: Install and set up (10 minutes)
lessons.lead: You do this once per computer.

items.title: Install Git
items.text: Download from **git-scm.com** and install with the default options. On a Mac, run *git --version* and accept the prompt.

items.title: Tell Git who you are
items.text: Use the SAME email as your GitHub account, so your commits are linked to you.

items.title: Create a GitHub account
items.text: Use a professional username (e.g. *kamal-perera*, not *xXcoolboyXx*). Employers will see it.

items.title: Sign in from your computer
items.text: The easiest way: sign in to GitHub inside VS Code, or install **GitHub Desktop**. Both handle login for you.

items.title: Check it works
items.text: Run *git --version* in a terminal. You should see a version number.

blocks.title: Terminal — run once
blocks.code:
git config --global user.name "Kamal Perera"
git config --global user.email "kamal@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git --version

lessons.title: How Git works: the 4 places your code lives
lessons.lead: Understand this picture and every Git command makes sense.

items: **Working folder** — the files you edit in VS Code.
**Staging area** — the changes you have picked for the next commit (*git add*).
**Local repository** — your saved commits, on your computer (*git commit*).
**GitHub (remote)** — the shared copy your team uses (*git push* sends, *git pull* receives).

blocks.text: A commit is NOT on GitHub until you **push**. If your laptop dies before you push, that work is gone. Push at least once a day.

lessons.title: Your first repository
lessons.lead: Two ways to start: create a new repo, or copy (clone) one your team already made.

items.bad: Create an empty repo on GitHub (New → name it → Create). Then in your project folder: git init → git add . → git commit -m "Initial commit" → git remote add origin <url> → git push -u origin main
items.good: Copy the repo URL from the green “Code” button on GitHub. Then: git clone <url> → cd <folder> → start working.
items.why: Only ONE person creates the repo. Everyone else clones it. Never copy project folders over USB or WhatsApp.

blocks.title: Start a new project
blocks.code:
cd my-project
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git remote add origin https://github.com/kamal-perera/findit.git
git push -u origin main

lessons.title: The everyday workflow
lessons.lead: Five commands cover 90% of daily Git. Learn this loop by heart.

items.title: Pull first
items.text: *git pull* — get your team’s latest work BEFORE you start.

items.title: Work
items.text: Edit code, run it, test it.

items.title: Check
items.text: *git status* — see what changed. *git diff* — see the exact lines.

items.title: Stage and commit
items.text: *git add <files>* then *git commit -m "Add login page"*.

items.title: Push
items.text: *git push* — share it with your team.

head: Command
What it does
When to use it
rows: Shows changed, staged and new files
All the time — it is always safe
Stages one file for the next commit
Saves a snapshot with a message
Downloads and merges your team’s changes
Shows the history, one line per commit
Shows exact line changes not yet staged

questions.q: You just made a commit. Can your teammate see it on GitHub?
questions.why: Commits are saved on your computer only. git push sends them to GitHub.

questions.q: What should you do FIRST when you sit down to work?
questions.why: Pull first so you build on top of your team’s latest code and avoid conflicts.

questions.q: Which command is always safe and shows what has changed?
questions.why: git status only reads — it never changes anything.

lessons.title: Write good commit messages
lessons.lead: A commit message tells the story of your project. Write it so your teammate understands it in 3 seconds.

blocks.text: Use the **imperative mood** — write it like a command: “**Add** login page”, not “Added login page” or “Adding login page”. A good test: the sentence *“If applied, this commit will …”* should make sense with your message at the end.

items.why: Says WHAT changed. “update” could mean anything.

items.good: Fix crash when the roadmap has no milestones
items.why: Describes the bug, so it can be found later.
Professional and searchable. Git already keeps versions — do not put versions in messages.

head: Prefix (Conventional Commits)
Use it for
Example
rows: feat: add deadlines calendar to roadmap page
fix: stop chat from scrolling the page
docs: add setup steps for PostgreSQL
test: add golden cases for planner agent
Code change that adds no feature and fixes no bug

do: Commit small, working steps (many commits per day is good)
Keep the first line under ~50 characters
One topic per commit
dont: Commit code that does not build
Mix 5 unrelated changes in one commit
Write messages like “asdf”, “wip”, “changes”

lessons.title: Branches: work without breaking things
lessons.lead: A branch is a safe copy of the code where you build one feature. When it works, you merge it back into main.

blocks.title: Branch commands
blocks.code:
git switch -c feature/login     # create a new branch and move to it
# ...work, add, commit...
git push -u origin feature/login # first push of this branch
git switch main                  # go back to main
git pull                         # get the latest main
git branch                       # list branches (* = current)

blocks.text: Golden rule for teams: **main must always work.** Nobody commits directly to main — every change arrives through a branch and a pull request.

head: Branch name
Good for
rows: If your module asks for student IDs in branch names

lessons.title: Team workflow and pull requests
lessons.lead: A pull request (PR) says: “Here are my changes — please check them before they go into main.”

items.title: Pick a task
items.text: Use a GitHub Issue or your project board so everyone knows who is doing what.

items.title: Create a branch
items.text: *git switch -c feature/task-name* from an up-to-date main.

items.title: Commit and push
items.text: Small commits, then *git push -u origin feature/task-name*.

items.title: Open a pull request
items.text: On GitHub click **Compare & pull request**. Explain what, why and how to test it. Add screenshots for UI changes.

items.title: Review
items.text: A teammate reads the code, tests it, and comments or approves.

items.title: Merge and clean up
items.text: Merge into main, delete the branch, and everyone runs *git pull*.

do: Keep PRs small — one feature each
Write a clear description (use our PR template)
Review kindly: suggest, do not insult
Link the issue: “Closes #12”
dont: Merge your own PR without anyone looking (unless your team agreed)
Leave PRs open for a week
Push straight to main
Approve without reading or running the code

lessons.title: Merge conflicts (don’t panic)
lessons.lead: A conflict happens when two people change the SAME lines. Git cannot guess which is right, so it asks you.

blocks.title: What a conflict looks like inside the file
blocks.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
const API_URL = 'http://localhost:5220';
=======
const API_URL = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;
>>>>>>> feature/env-config

items: Between **<<<<<<< HEAD** and **=======** is YOUR version.
Between **=======** and **>>>>>>>** is the OTHER version.
Keep the right code (or combine both), then delete all three marker lines.

items.title: Open the file
items.text: VS Code highlights conflicts and offers buttons: *Accept Current*, *Accept Incoming*, *Accept Both*.

items.title: Decide and edit
items.text: If unsure, ask the teammate who wrote the other version.

items.title: Test
items.text: Run the app. Make sure it builds and works.

items.title: Finish
items.text: *git add <file>* then *git commit* (or continue the merge).

blocks.text: Avoid most conflicts: **pull often, keep branches short (1–3 days), and split work by file or feature** so two people rarely edit the same lines.

lessons.title: What NEVER to commit (.gitignore and secrets)
lessons.lead: Some files must never go on GitHub: passwords, API keys, and huge generated folders.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: API keys, database passwords, .env files, appsettings.Local.json.

items.title: Generated folders
items.text: node_modules, bin, obj, dist, build — anyone can rebuild them.

items.title: Personal files
items.text: .vs, .idea, .DS_Store, log files.

blocks.text: A **.gitignore** file in the root of your repo lists patterns Git should ignore. Download our ready-made one from the **Templates** tab. For settings, commit an *example* file with fake values (e.g. *appsettings.Local.example.json*) so teammates know what to fill in.

If you ever push a real API key: **revoke/rotate the key immediately** on the provider’s website. Deleting the file in a new commit is NOT enough — the key is still in the history, and bots scan GitHub for keys within minutes.

blocks.title: Already committed a folder by mistake?
blocks.code:
# 1. add the folder to .gitignore, then:
git rm -r --cached node_modules
git commit -m "chore: stop tracking node_modules"
git push

lessons.title: Undo mistakes safely
lessons.lead: Almost everything in Git can be undone. Find your situation below.

head: Situation
Command
Safe for shared work?
rows: I want to throw away changes in one file (not committed)
I staged a file by mistake
Typo in my last commit message (not pushed yet)
Undo my last commit but keep the changes (not pushed)
Save unfinished work to switch branch

do: Use *git revert* for anything already pushed
Run *git status* before and after
Ask your team before rewriting shared history
dont: Use *git push --force* on main
Use *git reset --hard* unless you are sure you want to lose work
Delete the .git folder to “fix” things

lessons.title: GitHub Actions: automatic checks (CI)
lessons.lead: CI (continuous integration) builds and tests your code automatically on every push — so broken code is caught before it reaches main.

blocks.text: Put a YAML file in **.github/workflows/**. GitHub runs it on its own computers and shows a or next to every commit and pull request.

blocks.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml — .NET + React example
blocks.code:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: '8.0.x' }
      - run: dotnet build backend
      - run: dotnet test backend
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '20' }
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
        working-directory: web

blocks.text: A green CI badge and passing tests on every PR is strong evidence of **professional engineering practice** — mention it in your report and viva.

lessons.title: Make your repo examiner-ready
lessons.lead: Before you submit, your GitHub repository should look like a real, professional project.

items: README explains what it is, how to install, configure and run it (use our README template)
No passwords, API keys or .env files anywhere in the history
.gitignore is in place — no node_modules, bin or obj folders
main branch builds and runs from a fresh clone
Every team member has regular commits under their own name
Commit messages are clear and professional
Work went through branches and pull requests
CI (GitHub Actions) passes
Repo has a description, and the About section has topics
Final version is tagged (e.g. v1.0) or published as a Release

templates.name: Project proposal
templates.when: Before you start building — to get your idea approved.
inside: Problem statement and SMART objectives
Existing solutions table
Scope (in / out)
Tech stack with reasons
Timeline, risks and team roles

templates.name: Project plan & Gantt chart
templates.when: Week 1. Plan every phase and see it as a timeline.
inside: Tasks, owners, start week and length
Gantt bars draw themselves automatically
Status dropdown — done tasks turn light green
Week dates from your start date

templates.name: Risk register
templates.when: With your proposal, then update it every few weeks.
inside: Likelihood × impact score (automatic)
High risks turn red, medium amber
Mitigation, owner and status columns

templates.name: Requirements specification (SRS)
templates.when: After the proposal — before you design and code.
inside: Functional requirements table with IDs and MoSCoW priority
Non-functional requirements with how to measure them
User classes and user stories with acceptance criteria
Traceability table (requirement → design → test)

templates.name: Design document
templates.when: Before and during building. Update it when the design changes.
inside: Architecture diagram and design-decision table
Database tables and ER diagram
API endpoint table
UI, security and deployment design

templates.name: Literature review matrix
templates.when: While you read papers and existing systems.
inside: One row per source with IEEE reference
Main idea, method, strengths and gaps
Theme column to group sources when you write

templates.name: Test plan

inside: Test strategy by level (unit, API, UI, user)
Environment, entry and exit criteria

Defect tracking and schedule

templates.name: Test cases log
templates.when: Every time you test. Paste the summary into your report.
inside: Steps, test data, expected and actual result
Pass / Fail dropdown — rows turn green or red
Summary sheet with pass rate (automatic)

templates.name: Final project report
templates.when: Start in the middle of the project — not the last week.
inside: Every standard chapter, from Abstract to Appendices
Grey guidance in every section (incl. which tense to use)
Automatic table of contents and page numbers
Objectives-met table and team contribution table

templates.name: User manual
templates.when: Near the end — often an appendix of the final report.
inside: Getting started and system requirements
One section per task with numbered steps
Troubleshooting / FAQ table

templates.name: Weekly progress log
templates.when: Every Friday, 10 minutes. It makes the report and viva much easier.
inside: What I completed, learned and was blocked by
Hours spent and plan for next week
Evidence links (commits, screenshots)

templates.name: Meeting minutes
inside: Attendees and apologies
Discussion and decisions
Action items with owner, due date and status

templates.name: README for your repository
templates.when: Day 1 of the repo. Keep it updated.
inside: Features and tech stack table
Install, configure and run steps
Testing, project structure and team table

templates.name: Pull request template
templates.when: Save as .github/pull_request_template.md — GitHub fills it in for every PR.
inside: What, why and how to test
Screenshots section
Checklist: builds, tests pass, no secrets

templates.name: .gitignore (.NET, React, Flutter)
templates.when: Before your first commit. Rename it to .gitignore.
inside: Secrets (.env, appsettings.Local.json, keys)
.NET bin/obj, Node node_modules/dist

templates.when: For your final presentation. 10 slides ≈ 10 minutes.
inside: Proven 10-slide story: problem → solution → demo → results
Speaker notes on every slide: what to say and how long
Editable chart for your results
